subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS

speechtext:
The house in committee on Bill No. 212, to amend the Telegraphs Act-Mr. Marler-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
On clause 1-"External submarine cable" and "telecommunication" defined.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when this bill was up for second reading I explained the position being taken by the official opposition in the following words, as found at page 5617 of Hansard of July 3:
We in the official opposition are curious about some aspects of this particular bill and while we are not opposing it at this stage we are reserving our right to do so in the event that the examination by the committee reveals the bill has features which in our opinion would justify opposition to it in the subsequent stages.
In the interim the bill has been considered by the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, and as a result of the deliberations of that committee we believe that the government should take another look before insisting on, the passage of the bill. To us it appears to be designed to stifle competition with the crown company known as Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation, and we believe that Canadians are entitled to the benefit of competition, between this crown company and the private companies which are operating in the same field.
Furthermore, we are afraid that the enactment of this legislation and the policy behind the legislation will in due course lead to the crown company, Canadian, Overseas Telecommunication Corporation, having a monopoly in the field of external submarine cable service from Canada.
The bill will give the government a licensing power over outlets from these external submarine cables. In, addition it will give a licensing control over the routing of cable messages within Canada. The minister really explained that in his speech on second reading. I am referring to page 5616 of Hansard of July 3, where the minister said the following:
The government believes that by establishing a licensing system it will be in a better position to

Telegraphs Act
deal more flexibly with applications for permission to land cables, to control the opening of circuits into Canada, and to regulate increases in the capacity of cables; and the amendment before the house has been drafted with these objects in mind.
That goes further than the law at the present time. The Telegraphs Act, chapter 262 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, does give the government very wide control over the landing of cables in Canada. I do not believe any wider control would be possible, and we were told in the committee that in practice such control has always been recognized by the existing companies. But now the government is seeking to go further and take this licensing control over the circuits that come from the cable head. Also, as the minister said, as reported lower down on page 5616-

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: I think the hon. member is mistaken when he speaks about licensing control over circuits coming from the cable head. I think the hon. gentleman should recall that the bill deals only with the cables themselves, not with the circuits in Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext:
No. In the paragraph I have just read the minister himself explained the purpose of this bill. He said they were going to establish a licensing system under which:
. . . the government . . . will be in a better position to deal more flexibly with applications for permission to land cables-
They already had power to deal with the landing of cables. He then went on to say this:
-to control the opening of circuits into Canada, and to regulate increases in the capacity of cables: . . .
Further down on the same page we find this:
. . . but I think 1 should point out that the proposed licensing system would enable us to exercise some measure of control over the routing of traffic originating in Canada.
In the committee it was admitted by the minister that the main purpose of this amendment is to control competition from a reliable and long-established private company known as the Commercial Cable Company of Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: I think the hon. member is putting a very broad interpretation on what I said.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext:
I do not think I am putting a broad interpretation on it at all. I could quote half a dozen places in the evidence where the minister made it perfectly clear that the reason this amendment was being brought in was in order to permit him to control the outlets which the Commercial Cable Company of Canada would have.

That brings me to the plans of this private company. It has been in business in Canada since 1884, a period of 72 years. It is a United States company authorized by special statute of the parliament of Canada in 1884 to carry on this cable business in this country. It is a highly efficient organization. I am told by people who use the cable services of this company that it is the most efficient one in the field operating from the shores of Canada, and that when they wish to get fast service they mark their cables "via Commercial Cable".
This company have not laid a cable for about 33 years. Now they desire to lay what is known as a coaxial cable. I am not very well versed in the technical language of this business, Mr. Chairman; hence I may not get the accurate description in some cases. But evidently this is a modern, up to date type of cable. It is to extend from the United States through Canada, thence I think to Greenland and Iceland and then either to the United Kingdom or some country on the continent of Europe. There are to be what are known as 120 outlets.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: Duplex circuits; 120 duplex circuits.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext:
I thank the minister for his correction. Of that number, 24 are to be made available in Canada if this company is allowed to proceed with its plans. The company is trying to modernize its service. For example, one of the officials told us in the committee that the company had a request from a large firm in Vancouver for a direct service which could be given only if this coaxial cable is laid, something which would put Vancouver on a competitive basis with Montreal in so far as cables to the United Kingdom, for example, are concerned.
I personally see no reason why the businessmen of the west coast should be denied that advantage, or should be forced to do business with the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation, which is what will result if this bill goes through and the government does not change its policy. It was also said that there were demands for leased wire service from Vancouver which could not be met unless this cable could be laid. The same thing applies to Winnipeg, where the Winnipeg grain exchange is in direct competition with the Chicago grain exchange. The men in business there want to have this fast service. Apparently they have applied for such service, and can only get it through Commercial Cable if that company is allowed to lay this modern cable. Otherwise they too will be in the position of being forced to do business,

whether they wish to do so or not, with the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation.
Now, Commercial Cable told the committee that as far back as 1950 they decided that they had to lay a modern cable. They gave evidence that in 1953 they had discussed this whole question with the officials of the Department of Transport. I have here a copy of their brief, from which I shall quote.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: Was it not 1954?

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext:
No, they say here that they reported their intentions to the Canadian government officials in 1953.
There were delays caused by extensive surveys, plans and specifications, arranging for cable ships, arranging the $25 million financing and by change of route requested by government and other matters so that it was not until September of 1954 that all the plans, maps, specifications, financial arrangements, etc., were complete and filed with the Canadian government in a well prepared and complete application covering practically every detail. The Commercial Cable Company was to have 24 outlets in Canada available in this cable as needed over the years to come, to take care of the business from the Canadian Pacific Telegraph Company and clients of the Commercial Cable Company.
I should explain that this Commercial Cable does not send messages over land in Canada. They are carried by the Canadian Pacific Telegraph Company. This application was considered by the department for some time and in February, 1955, the minister wrote a letter to the solicitor for the company which 1 propose to read because it sets out the stand taken by the Department of Transport at that time. I think the same stand is being taken by the government today. The letter reads:
Dear Mr. Maclaren:
I refer to your letter of January 28, 1955, and previous correspondence in connection with the application of Commercial Cable Company to land on the coast of Canada a new trans-Atlantic coaxial cable.
The government is prepared, subject to compliance by the company with all statutory requirements, to grant authority for the landing of the proposed cable, subject to certain technical and related stipulations the details of which are now being worked out; and subject to the conditions-
This is the part of the letter that is significant and to which I wish to draw attention. -that no circuits shall be terminated in Canada except for:
(1)	Purposes of defence communication from Canada to points outside Canada, so far as other available circuits are insufficient,
(2)	Commercial purposes in respect of circuits leased to Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation.
In other words, this company could lay their cable in Canada and could have circuits in Canada only if those circuits were either for purposes of defence or were leased to
Telegraphs Act
this crown corporation. That tells the whole story right there. Are we in Canada to be put in this position with regard to external submarine cables? Then the letter went on:
The nature and extent of defence communications permitted under (1) above will be defined specifically following further consideration of defence needs.
As soon as the details of the above mentioned technical and related stipulations have been worked out, an order in council will be prepared to implement the foregoing.
The company were unwilling to comply with that letter, and frankly I do not blame them a bit. I think there are many hon. members in this house on the government side as well as in opposition parties who would not blame the company for being unwilling to lay a cable subject to those conditions.
They have complied with the law during the whole 72 years they have been doing business in Canada. They went to the government about this new cable landing and about their plans for circuits in Canada. Apparently they have always gone to the department about any rates that were to be charged. Whether or not they were under obligation to do so, the evidence showed that this had been their practice. They have done everything possible to co-operate with the government, but they now run up against this snag in that seven years ago the government set up a crown corporation and has apparently decided now that this government child, Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation, is to be shielded and protected from competition.
Evidence was given by the officials of the company to the effect that they have no objection whatever to a licensing system provided that the rights given them under their original incorporating bill are not nullified, and that the system is not exercised in favour of the crown corporation. They said furthermore that they have no objection to the control of cable rates. So much for Commercial Cable.
Then I come to the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation. It was set up in 1949 as the result of an agreement among different commonwealth companies. Canada took over the assets of two private companies; I think they were Cable and Wireless Limited and Marconi. Part of the agreement among the commonwealth companies was that those countries would resist -and that is the important word-the authorization or opening of new circuits which would be detrimental to Cable and Wireless Limited or its associates in the British empire.

Telegraphs Act
Those words appear in the agreement preceding the setting up of the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation. They seem to indicate that the policy of the government was to be one of monopoly or in any event of hamstringing the private companies, and that point was raised during the debate in this house in 1949. I will not quote again the extracts from Hansard which I read on July 3. There were also extracts from the proceedings of the committee, the same standing committee which dealt with the bill in that year. The then minister of transport, Hon. Mr. Chevrier, made it clear there was to be no interference with competition and that this crown company was not to have a monopoly.
But now after these intervening years we seem to have arrived at the point where that policy has been thrown overboard, and the government is adopting a policy which at least is severely restricting competition and which may result in monopoly, because if the private companies cannot modernize their systems it is only a matter of time until they will be out of the business as serious competitors.
The C.O.T.C. also felt that its facilities should be modernized, and this crown company made an agreement with the British post office and with another private United States company, the American Telephone and Telegraph Company, which as hon. members know is a very powerful United States utility. Another party to the agreement was the Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company, which is a subsidiary of the American Telephone and Telegraph Company. If hon. members care to check that agreement they will find a reference to it in chapter 77 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1953-54.
That is described as an act respecting the Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company. The recital sets out the various changes in the share capital of that company, and then the following recital appears:
.	.	. whereas the company pursuant to its
statutory powers is a party to a contract executed on the 27th day of November, 1953-
This was about the same time that Commercial Cable were talking with officials of the department.
-with Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation-	.
That is the crown company.
-American Telephone and Telegraph Company, and the Postmaster General of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland for the construction and maintenance of a transAtlantic telephone cable system for service between Canada and the United Kingdom and between the United States and the United Kingdom, the execution of which contract by Canadian Overseas 
Telecommunication Corporation was approved on November 26, 1953, by order of the governor in council.
I am not quarrelling with the C.O.T.C. for making a contract of that kind. By the way, this new cable system is to be in operation this fall. I have in my hand the annual report of the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation for the year ending March 31, 1956, and on page 6 I find the following reference to transatlantic cables:
The installation of the trans-Atlantic telephone cable, in which the corporation is a joint owner with the British post office, American Telephone and Telegraph Company and Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company, should be completed and its services in operation by the end of October next-some few weeks earlier than originally anticipated. We look forward to its inauguration with considerable enthusiasm as we believe it to be the most important overseas telecommunication development since the laying of the original telegraph cable over ninety years ago. Our share in this cable will provide for Canada services and facilities for which there has been a steadily increasing need during recent years. In addition to high quality telephone service, we shall offer picture transmissions-broadcast programs- customer-to-customer teleprinter services-leased telegraph circuits for the use of private customers and we shall also introduce a multiplicity of new telegraph circuits in sufficient numbers to meet adequately the needs of Canadian users for some years to come. We are confident that the services so being provided will take care of foreseeable public demands and that the users will be completely satisfied with the quality and quantity of service available to them.
The question we ask is why should the other company be prevented by means of a government licensing system from inaugurating a service of that kind.
The minister explained in the committee that this new transatlantic cable would provide six new circuits for Canada. He indicated that number would be adequate for Canadian needs. He went on to say that the C.O.T.C. now has 40 per cent of the Canadian cable business and he wants it to get more, and that is one reason that this licensing control over the private companies is being taken. The minister said he objected to any more facilities; that these six circuits are ample, and he objected to any more circuits of that kind. He claimed further that his department should have the power to decide whether there was or was not any duplication of services, and whether this private company should be able to establish service of the kind I have just mentioned.
He said also that the department wanted to control the routing of cables in Canada. I think that would be a pretty tough job, because a company could send its cables via the United States. For example, a firm in Vancouver might be forced to send its cables across the United States. The minister is trying to force business into the hands of

C.O.T.C. The Vancouver Province summed up the situation very neatly on July 21, just a few days ago, in the following editorial: Mr. Marler's Blackjack is Showing
Despite the federal government's efforts to conceal its growing autocracy under a cloak of benign and democratic tolerance, the bulge of the government's blackjack can be glimpsed at unexpected moments.
We had such a glimpse last week when suave and friendly transport minister Marler was explaining to a parliamentary committee that his legislation to control operation of overseas cable service in Canada is not aimed at pushing out the private companies and creating a monopoly for the government-owned operation.
Why, said Mr. Marler, if we wanted to do that we could simply expropriate their property and close them out.
This is quite true. But it might have been better if Mr. Marler's frankness had not been carried quite so far.
Canadians have had a convincing demonstration this year of how a top-heavy majority in the House of Commons has encouraged the government to do all sorts of things, including forcing a Speaker to stay in office after he had resigned. Such shows of power can be frightening.
Furthermore, the C.O.T.C. has been not only a competitor but a judge in this whole matter. I should like to refer to page 6 of the brief submitted by Commercial Cable. In describing a meeting which took place in the offices of the Department of Transport in September, 1954, they say:
At the meeting there were some 16 men, four delegates from the Department of Transport, four from the Commercial Cable Company, one, who acted as secretary, from the privy council as the application was necessarily addressed to the governor general in council. Among the others, it is interesting to note that there were three representatives from Canadian Overseas Telecommunications Corporation (C.O.T.C.), including its president, to whom nearly everything said was referred for his comment or approval. There was also a representative, a Lieutenant Colonel Read, from the B.P.O.-Cable and Wireless (of Great Britain). C-O-T.C. and Cable and Wireless are direct competitors of the Commercial Cable Company and they were sitting in judgment upon this application.
Then further down:
Mr. Bowie, president of C.O.T.C., the crown corporation which is a competitor, undertook to look over the application and give the Department of Transport his opinion.
That sort of interference must be stopped if there is to be competition in this field.

speechtext: Those are wholly unsupported statements, are they not?

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: I do not believe these men are lying; there is no evidence to show that the men who drew up this brief are not telling the truth.

The C.O.T.C. is both competitor and judge. That is the key to the situation. That is a picture which should make hon. members pause and consider before allowing this bill to go on the statute books.
The minister argued in the committee that Commercial Cable was a United States concern and that he was all for Canadian companies. That was a somewhat surprising argument after the pipe-line debate; however, it was made. I merely point out that Commercial Cable is not obtaining any financial support from the government. It intends to build the cable with its own money. That was not the position in the pipe-line situation.
It was said also that this new cable proposed by the private company was to be subsidized in part by the United States defence department, which was to pay annually $1,600,000. I have no way of checking that, but I doubt very much whether American Telephone and Telegraph Company has not received the same or perhaps greater assistance in the way of fees from the United States department of defence. Certainly you have on the one side Commercial Cable and, on the other side, American Telephone and Telegraph Company. If the argument is to be based upon whether the company is a United States company then the department is not in any better position than the private company, because it is involved directly and very heavily with this other large United States corporation.
I suggest that the department take a second look at this whole policy. I see no reason why competitors should be hampered in this way. I think it is to the detriment of the Canadian people. The businessmen of Canada are entitled to the best service they can get. If companies put in too many circuits or more circuits than can be used now, no one is going to be hurt except those companies, and it certainly will not do any harm to Canadian businessmen. This policy adopted by the government seems to me to be far removed from what we have been led to believe was Liberal policy.
I hope the minister will not try to force this amendment through at the present time, but will take another look at it. Certainly the arguments against it are strong. It may be that as the result of a second look some policy can be worked out which will bring about a position where there is fair competition. Surely that is not going to do any harm to this crown company. There is no

reason why here in Canada we should be loading the dice for crown corporations. This is similar to the situation that would have been created if the government had taken licensing power over the railroads and then had said to the C.P.R., "You can run a railroad but you cannot have any diesel locomotives." That would be a similar situation, and for the life of me I cannot see any reason for a policy of that kind.

My colleagues and I who were on the committee went to that committee with an open mind. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni intimated that we would listen very carefully to the arguments put forward by Commercial Cable, Western Union and all the members of the committee. After weighing the evidence very carefully, we decided that on balance we would support the government position rather than the position outlined by the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra.
Before the committee during our last sitting, the hon. member for York West said he wished to deal with one point because he knew he would be confronted with it by the time this bill got into the house and that someone would say, "You are going to see that a big United States company is favoured in connection with a Canadian enterprise. I think if this were a Canadian enterprise working as I know it can, there would be no problem such as we are faced with today; there would be no need to come into this room." But the members of this committee are in the position that a powerful United States corporation is challenging the right of the Canadian parliament to make regulations that will affect the operation of this company that was granted a charter some 72 years ago.
Counsel for Commercial Cable seriously claimed that because they were given these privileges as far back as 1884, they would be permitted now in 1956 to do exactly as they choose in this important field. They are questioning the right of the minister to interfere with their plans in any way. Since the people of Canada are interested in C.O.T.C., I do not believe we can be asked to put this very powerful United States corporation in a preferred position.
I think the minister did a very good job in committee. He listened very patiently for long periods when able counsel for Commercial Cable presented a brief and made some arguments which appeared fairly convincing. They took us back to the famous trans-Canada pipe line and reminded us that we were prepared to offer a subsidy to this corporation. As a matter of fact they claimed

they were prepared to go into this deal without any subsidy from the Canadian taxpayer.
But the Minister of Transport drew our attention to something which did not appear in the brief. He reminded us that this company has a guarantee from the United States government of $1,600,000 per year for the next ten years, with an option to have that guarantee extended for a longer period. The minister quite correctly said, I think, that when one examines the situation with regard to cables, the word "subsidy" could be loosely applied to the proposed cable to a much greater degree than to any other project that has come before the parliament of Canada this session. The minister did not argue that this $1,600,000 was a subsidy, but counsel for Commercial Cable did not deny the fact that because this could be considered partially as a defence project, Uncle Sam's government was prepared to put into the exchequer of this company $1,600,000 per year for the next ten years.
That becomes a matter of concern to Canadian taxpayers because, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra pointed out, we have a considerable investment in the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation, and the last annual report we have had shows a net profit for the period of $217,000. I should like to speak on this bill for just a moment or two, Mr. Chairman. First I should like to ask the committee what are the reasons for this bill. There must be some reason which the government have in mind in introducing an amendment to change the legislation so they would have some means of knowing what was taking place with regard to communication cables laid to another continent.
In 1884 we find that the Commercial Cable Company applied to this parliament for a permit to lay a cable from here to England. That permit was granted. At that time they felt it wise to have certain powers, and one of them was the control of the price of the services rendered by these cables. The price was set at 25 cents per word. Let us look at the price paid for service over this cable today. The price is 15 cents per word. We have been paying some 5 or 6 cents less per word than the cost of sending a word from the United States on the same cable. I should like to suggest to the committee that one of the main reasons for Canadians getting that advantage of 5 or 6 cents per word is that we formed the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation back in 1949 and because of the control the Canadian government had over sending messages, by means of competition, thus keeping the price to Canadian users at 5 or 6 cents per word less than people in the United States pay.
In my opinion this is a good thing. However, so far as the powers of the government to control are concerned in relation to the agreement made in 1884, they are of very little value. The price which was set at that time, 25 cents per word, is now unrealistic. How did that come about? Well, I think it would be wise to look through the brief and the minutes of the committee to find some of the reasons. In 1884 this company asked for permission to lay cables, and in that year laid two cables. In 1894 they laid another one; another in 1904; a fifth in 1905 and a sixth in 1923. Then we were told in the committee that one of these cables went out of commission, so at the present time they have only five cables.
We are informed that these five cables have some 91 duplex channels. I think at this time it would be well for me to say what a duplex channel is. It is a circuit which provides for

the transmission of two messages simultaneously, one in each direction. Now, how do they get 9i duplex circuits available in five cables? In the past 10 or 11 years there has been a great deal of experimental work done with communications. It has been found that by putting undersea repeaters on these cables they could double the capacity of the cables; by putting on tandem repeaters they could square the capacity. There is no doubt that with further experimentation the time will come when they can cube the number of messages on a single cable.
Has our government any knowledge of the increased capacity that has taken place in these cables that this company was given permission to lay years ago? That they have no knowledge of what these increases are, and they have no way of finding out other than through the willingness of the company to give them that information. I would point out the embarrassing position in which our minister found himself, as shown by the committee evidence at page 206 when, after having made a statement to the committee from his official record of the number of circuits, the companies communicated with him during the night and informed him that they had many more circuits than he had put on the record. Mr. Chairman, the whole problem presented by this bill is very complicated, as I think the minister and all hon. members who sat on this committee would agree. We heard a great deal of evidence in the committee dealing with a highly technical subject which naturally for the layman was difficult to follow; but having had the opportunity to read over the evidence which was given before the committee and having had some time in which to consider it, I find there are certain points that make themselves evident.
There is a fear in the minds of at least some hon. members of the opposition parties that despite what the minister said concerning monopoly, such a situation will develop. I believe the minister referred to this four times. At page 202 of No. 4 of the minutes and proceedings of the committee the minister used words to the effect that the government had no intention whatever of setting up any kind of monopoly, either directly or indirectly. While the minister may have said that, and no one would question his integrity, there no doubt will be other ministers of transport after the present one, and they may have a different view; and the cabinet may, of course, change its opinion in this respect from time to time.
It is the fear of certain hon. members of the opposition that the powers under this act would enable the government, if it desired to do so, to set up a monopoly for the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation, which many of us would not like to see happen. We have seen government monopolies in the C.B.C., Trans-Canada Air Lines and in other fields. Although I know some hon. members feel these are perfectly all right there are a great many people, and I would be almost inclined to say a majority of the people in this country, who do not favour government monopolies of this type. It is exactly because of this fear that another government monopoly may be set up or may be experiencing birth at the present time that we raise objection to this particular piece of legislation.
The situation at the present time seems to be somewhat as follows. The present cable companies such as the Commercial Cable corporation and Western Union may replace existing outlets-

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: Existing cables.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext:
-may replace existing cables. Thank you, Mr. Minister. I understand they may not put down any new ones. The minis-

ter has just said that they may replace existing cables, and I know that in the committee we had a great deal of discussion about just what the word "outlet" means. As I understand the position at the present time it is that these companies may replace existing cables but they may not replace these cables with a new kind of cable. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra pointed out in his remarks, I think it is very much the same as allowing the railways to replace wood-burning locomotives with diesels, because the new coaxial cables will apparently carry a great many more messages than the old type of cable that was laid down 50 or 75 years ago, when these cables were originally put down.
While the minister has just said that the government has no desire to regulate the additional number of outlets, I would like the minister to think over that statement because I am not certain that is exactly what he meant.
One objection to the minister's remarks that he heard throughout the committee proceedings was that the minister had indicated he was worried over the fact that the Commercial Cable corporation would have 24 additional outlets if these coaxial cables were laid down, and the minister felt this might endanger competition with the C.O.T.C. and even with Western Union.
Those hon. members of this house who were on the committee will recall that the witness for the Commercial Cable corporation pointed out that the reason they were making these additional outlets available for Canadian business was because they felt from their experience and as a result of investigations that the cable business in Canada would warrant these additional outlets within the next few years because Canada is a large and expanding country. We have certainly heard from hon. members in this house and particularly those on the government side about what a large and expanding economy we have, that things are fine and business is good. One witness for Commercial Cable pointed out that Canada had become a great commercial nation, and that to meet the needs of this modern and speedy world it was necessary to get in bids in order to purchase goods abroad in a hurry, and that service was demanded to meet these needs. Reference was made to many new types of service, the names of which I cannot recall, but I do remember reference to teletype and that sort of thing. For this reason it was felt that additional outlets would be necessary in the immediate future to carry on Canadian business.

The minister seemed to be concerned during the debate as to the effect of these outlets, and contended that they were not necessary at the present time. He seemed to be worried about the effect these additional outlets would have on the cable business. I was curious about that and asked him to explain, and I should like to quote from page 189 of the proceedings of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. I asked the minister if the government had the power to control the rates on telecommunications, and the minister replied, as reported on page 189 of the proceedings, as follows:
There are some provisions in the Telegraphs Act, but I am told there was a question as to whether they are effective inasmuch as they do not seem in their terms to extend beyond the territorial limits of Canada. There is also a provision in the Railway Act which would give jurisdiction to the board of transport commissioners over cable rates. My understanding is that that section of the act has not been proclaimed.
The minister has expressed doubt as to whether the government has authority to regulate rates for telecommunications at the present time, but I would think from the minister's statement that there would be no doubt that the government has authority. Last evening we heard something about jurisdiction over territorial waters. A cable must touch the mainland of Canada and to do so must come through Canadian territorial waters. In order to touch down at a mythical point, as we used to say in geometry, it would have to pass through at least three miles of Canadian territorial waters. Therefore the government would certainly have the power to legislate as to rates to be charged.
Then the minister said that the provision in the Railway Act which gave the board of transport commissioners power to regulate rates had not been proclaimed. I asked the minister whether it was intended to proclaim that section of the act, and he replied that they were quite satisfied that competition was keeping rates down at the present time.
Speaking of competition, the minister seemed to be concerned over the fact that Commercial Cable would receive an annual rental fee of $1,600,000 from the United States government, apparently for the carrying of defence messages or something of that nature. The minister felt that this would act as an indirect form of subsidy to that cable company which would put Commercial Cable in a better position than either C.O.T.C. or possibly Western Union. That seemed a little incomprehensible to me so I asked the minister certain questions about it, and I quote again from page 189 of the proceedings:

I would say in that connection, since you are in doubt as to whether any existing regulation would regulate rates by either the
Telegraphs Act
board of transport commissioners or anybody else, that there is a possibility; and one of the things which worries the government would be that because of the form of the subsidy to the Commercial Cable Company, that they might be able to engage in a rate war or something like that.

speechtext: Perhaps I should put it to you this way-that while the rates may be uniform the amount which might be spent to attract business might be greater in one case than another.

speechtext: I see, you mean for advertising?

Yes, or the amount paid under the traffic agreements might be greater in one case than in another. I am not suggesting that the company would do these things, but there is the possibility which I think should be considered at the same time that one talks about rates.
I think that shows quite clearly that this indirect form of subsidy to the Commercial Cable Company would not put them in a better position to operate in Canada, in other words to give unfair competition to C.O.T.C. or to Western Union or whoever may be their successors. I am afraid I cannot quite follow that line of reasoning, because cable messages are handled in this country by either Canadian National or Canadian Pacific telegraphs. If a message is sent by Canadian National I understand it is transmitted by Western Union; if it is picked up by Canadian Pacific it is sent either by Commercial Cable or Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation. When the average person goes to send an overseas cable he goes to the telegraph office with which he is accustomed tc deal. If he usually deals with the C.N. he goes to the C.N.; if he usually deals with the C.P., he goes there. The average person in this country does not know how his message is transmitted overseas. I doubt very much if hon. members of this committee, with the exception of those who happened to be on the standing committee, know that Commercial Cable Company carry Canadian Pacific messages and Western Union carry Canadian National messages.
To say that advertising done by Commercial Cable Company in Canada is going to encourage people to go to the C.P. office and say, "I want my message sent by Commercial Cable," or to go to the C.N. office and say, "I do not want to deal with the Canadian National because I want my messages to go by Commercial Cable," is rather hard to believe when the rates are the same. It does not make any sense. Sending a cable is somewhat like making a telephone call; provided the rates are the same you send it from the most convenient place.
If there is any fear in the mind of the minister that rates would not be kept the same by competition because of this indirect subsidy, control over rates could be exercised by the means mentioned by the minister. If it were thought that the amounts paid

Telegraphs Act
under traffic agreements were greater in one case than m the other; it either of these companies started to do that; if Commercial Cable started to do that, I submit that the board of transport commissioners could easily be given the power to control cable rates. Freight rates are controlled and nobody objects or considers it improper. If similar action appeared to be necessary in connection with telecommunications rates, similar action could be taken. We have never had evidence in the past that such action was necessary.
Changing the subject slightly, I should like to suggest that the purpose of these regulations is simply to protect the Canadian Overseas Telecommunications Corporation. One does not like to make statements when they are based on meagre evidence, but I have made inquiries at various telegraph offices and the information I have received is that at the present time-I am not saying that the service may not be improved in the future-the service provided by C.O.T.C. is not quite as good as that provided by Commercial Cable.
I asked what they meant by that. They said, "The message is sent and we have to follow it up" or "It has gone to the wrong address." "If we are dealing with Commercial Cable corporation we have no difficulty in following up the matter, but if we are dealing with C.O.T.C. it is difficult to trace the messages, and the service generally does not seem as good." This is a matter that can easily be corrected. It may be only a temporary thing. It may only have been the experience of the particular people I have asked about this, but it is indicative and it is something that is worth considering.
Because of the fact that the government apparently does not intend to allow these other companies to have additional outlets, I feel that this cannot but protect the C.O.T.C. Even if it is not a government monopoly at the moment, I cannot see how anything but this can result. If a company which has cables that have been laid 50 or 60 years ago, as the case may be, is going to replace these cables and it can only replace them with the same kind of cable, it is not very economical to do so. I think the old example of the replacement of the wood-burning engine with the diesel applies. I do not think it is reasonable for the government to expect that any commercial cable company would replace an old, antiquated type of cable with the same type. No doubt the cable company would simply say, "If we are to replace our 1883 cable with the same type of cable, when science has advanced so much since 1883, we are simply not going to do it." If these companies cannot put down modern cables when

the time comes to replace them, I doubt very much if they would do anything else. Eventually a government monopoly would be set up.
There are one or two other matters which I would like to touch upon briefly. As indicted at page 202 of the report of the committee's proceedings the minister stated very clearly and without reservations that the government had no intention of setting up a monopoly. I was glad to hear that. However, as recorded at page 143 of the same report, I asked Mr. Corlett, who was the counsel for the Commercial Cable Company, the following question:

I would say. theoretically, that is quite possible.
The minister made a reply to that, as recorded on page 180 of the proceedings. It reads as follows:
Now, somebody seemed to think this morning that it would be possible that we might introduce discriminatory regulations. AH I can say is: I do not think that in the whole of the history of Canada there has ever been a government which has so abused the power to make regulations as in fact to discriminate against one corporation in favour of some other corporation. I think it is perfectly clear that, if any such action were taken by any government, it would not long command the respect and support of the majority of the members of the House of Commons. I say that, regardless of which party may be in power. I fully realize that in theory one may adopt what would appear to be discriminatory provisions in the regulations but I cannot believe that the present government, or any future government, is going to adopt that action under this legislation.
That sounds very well, but when one considers that statement by the minister, while it is not exactly the same situation, one cannot help thinking of the C.B.C. and possibly certain other crown companies. Possibly Trans-Canada Air Lines has a somewhat preferred position over certain other air lines. Those are not exactly analogous, but they are close enough to bring the thought to one's mind. It may not be the intention, and since the minister has said so I am quite willing to accept his word that it is not the intention to do so at the present time. One cannot help feeling that in the future, once the pattern is set for legislation of this kind, the opportunity is there for somebody else to

do it in the future, and the present government certainly has the idea in mind of indulging in, we should say, the luxury of crown corporations. We have seen plenty of evidence of that, and I think that is one reason a number of the members of this house, including myself, are worried and suspicious about this legislation.
Finally, the hon. member for Wellington South in his remarks, which were in many ways enlightening and interesting, said he thought the reason for this legislation was that the government had the right to know how many cable outlets there were in and out of Canada. No one would quarrel with the hon. member in that statement. Of course the government has the right to know that, and I do not think anybody would disagree with him about that, but is that the whole intention of this?

Mr. Chairman, to finish the remarks I was making before we adjourned for the noon recess, I should like to close
Telegraphs Act
with a thought I have already mentioned several times, namely that the minister seemed greatly concerned and, in fact, his chief reason for refusing permission to the Commercial Cable corporation to land its proposed coaxial cable was the fact that the company was to receive an annual guaranteed rental of $1,600,000 a year for 10 years from the United States government. As I have already mentioned, the reason was given that this was in effect a form of subsidy which would give the Commercial Cable corporation a possible advantage over Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation and even Western Union. I think I have touched on the various reasons why I do not agree with the minister that this is correct, but there is one more point I should like to make in this respect before I take my seat.
It was suggested in the committee that the minister would certainly be able to call into being the section of the Railway Act which would enable the government to control rates for overseas cables. I have not the quotation in front of me and if I am wrong I am quite sure the minister will correct me, but at that time the minister implied that he thought competition was a better way than regulation to deal with the rates.
I mentioned earlier in my remarks that I do not think that necessarily follows, because Canadian railway rates are regulated and no one has any complaint about that. But even in the event that the board of transport commissioners do not want to take the power to regulate overseas telecommunication rates I think that the Commercial Cable corporation is in no better position than C.O.T.C., let us say, because of the $1,600,000 a year for 10 years by way of guaranteed rent that they are to get from the United States government.
The answer is this. Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation undoubtedly and unquestionably has government loans or funds at its disposal if necessary. Last year C.O.T.C. received a loan of $6 million. As the minister pointed out at page 198 of the report of the proceedings of the committee, C.O.T.C. paid interest on the loan. That is quite true. We would expect they would. But if C.O.T.C. were faced in the future with a rate war or needed money for capital expansion or anything else, I have very little doubt that they would get any loan they required to carry on business and meet any competition.
As I pointed out to the minister in the committee, knowing that it is very doubtful if any private company in its right mind

Telegraphs Act
would attempt to start a rate war with the financial power of the Canadian government behind C.O.T.C. It was mentioned in the committee that we would not want to subsidize C.O.T.C. in order that it could give cheaper rates. I do not think that will ever be necessary. No private company, no matter how big it may be, is as big as the government. Commercial Cable or Western Union or Western Union's successor would never attempt any kind of rate war with C.O.T.C., because the boards of directors of those companies know perfectly well what would happen and would never set out on such a course. I think it is ridiculous to suggest that they would. I bring that last thought to mind in answer to the minister's objection to granting a landing licence for the proposed new cable of Commercial Cable corporation.
To sum up, in the first place the fact is that C.O.T.C. could, if necessary, get whatever loans it required. Second, the board of transport commissioners could regulate the rates if there were any question of a rate war. Third, even with the advantage that the minister suggests Commercial Cable would have because of this form of subsidy from the United States government, I do not see how that could be used to channel all the business into the new line of communication that Commercial Cable proposes, because in sending cablegrams advertising would have very little effect for the reasons I pointed out earlier. For the reasons I and my colleagues have set out we cannot agree to this legislation.

Mr. Chairman, I too was a member of that committee, but my mind is in the same state as that of

the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. I should like to say a few words on this simple little bill amending the Telegraphs Act which apparently involves a controversial subject. I should like to read the new section 41 set out in clause 1 of the bill. It is in these words:
41. No person shall in Canada
(a)	operate an external submarine cable; or
(b)	construct, alter, maintain or operate any works or facilities for the purpose of operating an external submarine cable
except under and in accordance with a licence issued under this part.
No doubt there are not too many in the house who have too much intimate knowledge about the matter of submarine cables. However, many of us have read accounts of the hazards encountered by those early adventurers who laid the first submarine cables across the vast expanses of the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. The first of these cables was laid between England and France in 1850, and after several attempts were made the first submarine cable was laid across the Atlantic in 1856. By 1928 there were 21 submarine cables spanning the Atlantic ocean.
We might think that with the advent of radio and radio communication around the world, submarine cables would have become obsolete. However, with the increase in international trade and the development of diplomatic services throughout the world there is an indication of a necessity for more submarine cables.
There have been a great many changes made in the types of cable used since the first cable was laid and also in the techniques that can be used to increase the efficiency and capacity of the cables already laid. The latest type seems to be the coaxial cable, which will take not only cable messages but telephone voice conversations, television pictures and so forth. However, although there are 21 or more of the older types of cables across the Atlantic, there are only a limited number of companies that will be affected by the new amending bill, No. 212.
All these companies have been operating for many years under special charters given to them by this parliament under the provisions of the Telegraphs Act, which was brought into force in 1875. Therefore in the first place it is rather hard to understand why the bill is necessary, when the companies have had to comply with all the terms of their own charters as well as with the terms of the Telegraphs Act, one provision of which reads as follows:
22. The company shall not exercise any of the powers by this part conferred until
(a) the company has submitted to the governor in council, a plan and survey of the proposed

site and location of such telegraph and its approaches at the shore, and of its stations, offices and accommodations on land and of all the intended works thereto appertaining, . . .
Let us look into the history of one of these companies that will be affected by this bill. Probably the one with the most business is the one owned by the government themselves, namely C.O.T.C. This was a government company that was formed as a crown corporation by act of this government in 1949, which brought about the amalgamation of two companies, one called the Marconi Company and the other Cable and Wireless Limited. I should like to say that the move that was made at that time to nationalize commonwealth telecommunication services resulted in control of the cable system to the extent of some 80 per cent by the British government-this was brought out in the evidence in 1949-a fact which would certainly strengthen the position of the crown corporation; and it is understood that at the present time they control 40 per cent of the Canadian business.
In 1953 this crown corporation began plans which will be finished in 1956 for the laying of one of the most modern and most efficient types of coaxial cables across the Atlantic. No doubt this will increase and speed up the service they are able to give, and will give them a decided advantage over other companies in the business.
Enough for the government crown corporation. Let us look for a moment at one of the private companies affected, namely Commercial Cable company. This is a company which has been in business for many years in Canada, since they were given a charter in 1884 by the government. No doubt they did much of the spade work in making available to all the people and corporations in Canada the advantage of overseas telecom-munciation services. Their cables were laid, one in 1884, one in 1894, one in 1900, one in 1905 and the latest in 1943. I might say that this company is manned and managed in Canada entirely by Canadians.
Back about 1950 the Commercial Cable company, having great faith in the possibilities of Canada as the fastest growing nation in the world, realized it needed new cables of the improved coaxial type in order to take care of the increased demands upon its services. In 1953 they reported their intentions to the Canadian government. But according to section 22 of the Telegraphs Act which I just read they had to submit all their plans and specifications to the governor in council for his approval.
This they did in September, 1954, after extensive delays caused by extensive surveys, change of the route requested by the
Telegraphs Act
government, financing and other matters, in a well prepared and complete application covering practically every detail. They were to have 24 outlets in Canada available as needed over the years to come. All such new business as was obtained would be at rates controlled by the transport department of the government of Canada. A meeting was arranged at which the cable company would present their case. They were told by the chairman, even before the application was considered, that they could not do what they wanted to do. At this meeting the advice of the president of C.O.T.C., the crown corporation which is in competition, was asked. Nothing further was decided at this meeting.
After six months of argument, permission was given to land on the coast of Canada and to pass through, but the Commercial Cable company was denied outlets in Canada except those requested by the crown corporation or those that were necessary for defence. This was a company that was willing to risk its own capital and which would leave hundreds of thousands of dollars in Canada annually. Some reference was made in the committee to the point that this was a wholly controlled United States company. I wonder why the Minister of Trade and Commerce does not rise in their defence. This is a United States company willing to provide service in Canada for Canadians at no cost to Canadian taxpayers, with no request for any loans or assistance from the Canadian government. Yet its application is being denied because the minister believes it will create unnecessary duplication of telegraph facilities. In this connection I should like to quote from a recent letter in the Globe and Mail which reads as follows:
This is the situation:
A new cable is being laid now-it will be ready in a matter of months-by the British government and American Telegraph and Telephone, primarily for telephone use, but with some telegraph circuits. Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation will get the use of six of those circuits. Transport Minister Marler said there is no demand in sight for any more.
Commercial Cable company says there is. It says it has five customers anxious to get leased circuits-private lines, in effect-and business on hand for seven to ten more. It doesn't think any of the 24 would go begging for traffic. Mr. Marler says that any more than the six the crown company is to get would mean unnecessary duplication of facilities.

Mr. Chairman, I was just trying to indicate that this bill is an indication that the government is creating a monopoly in this field, when C.O.T.C. is given special privileges and these same privileges are denied to other private companies to such an extent that C.O.T.C., by the addition of their new, more efficient coaxial cable can squeeze out by reduced costs and hence reduced rates, fair and just competition.
In the evidence given in the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines we have from Mr. Alistair Macdonald, counsel and solicitor for Western Union Telegraph Company, a statement which shows just how they feel about this matter.

destroy, the present lawful international telegraph operations of Western Union; and, in fact, such power could be used to effect a confiscation of Western Union's existing contract rights and legislative grants, thus, additionally, rendering valueless all plant, equipment and other assets validly established in Canada under applicable law stretching back over decades.

This trans-Atlantic telegraph cable to which I have just referred will, as has been stated earlier, be finished early in October, and I think it will be going into service at approximately that time. It was in the light of those facts that the application of the Commercial Cable company had to be considered.
I wish to emphasize particularly that the proposals of the Commercial Cable company contemplated the laying of a cable which would have a capacity of 120 duplex circuits. So far as we understood the matter, whilst it was possible that two voice circuits would be used, which would take up approximately 24 of the duplex circuits, for telephone purposes, we have been inclined to consider it as a cable project rather than as a telephone project. Of the 120, 24 of these duplex circuits were to be terminated in Canada.
I should like hon. members to appreciate exactly the significance of that figure of 24. The capacity to which I have been referring and which is being used. The 34 existing duplex circuits carry all the present cable business between the United States and Canada at the western end and the continent of Europe at the eastern end. I should like hon. members to note that here we have 34 circuits to carry all that business, and now the Commercial Cable company asks that we should permit it to terminate in Canada 24 more duplex channels, which in itself is almost as much-not quite as much-as the whole of the present installed cable capacity in the north Atlantic.
The information I have is that the Canadian business of Commercial Cable can be carried fairly efficiently on one duplex circuit. That may be too conservative an estimate, and it may be that two duplex circuits are required. It may be the fact that it can route messages down to New York and put them on the cable at the New York end. This perhaps means that one duplex circuit, strictly speaking, takes care of what might be called the strictly Canadian traffic that moves on to the cable, but whether it is one or two is, I think, not material. I wish to point out that the application of Commercial Cable is to open 24 circuits in Canada, in addition to the 11 duplex circuits that C.O.T.C. will be putting into operation in October of this year.
Before I finish with the Commercial Cable application, I should just like to mention one
Telegraphs Act
or two factors that were, let us say, glossed over this morning by the members of the Progressive Conservative party. The fact remains that this 120 duplex channel cable, which Commercial Cable proposed to lay if its application were granted, was to be in receipt of $1,600,000 per annum for circuits to be rented to the United States government. The project was strongly urged upon us as being necessary for the defence both of the United States and Canada and of the United Kingdom. Had it not been for that fact, I think it would not have gone as far as it actually did go. But, as was pointed out this morning, this cable was to start from the United States, touch in Canada, first in Nova Scotia and then go across to Newfoundland, then go to Greenland, then to Iceland and then to the United Kingdom. Consequently, there were a number of governments whose approval and consent had to be obtained.
I am not in a position to divulge all of the information we received in that connection, but I should like to emphasize first of all that all of the governments were impressed with the desirability of the cable for defence purposes and for that reason gave, somewhat unwillingly, I think, a limited form of approval to the project. So far as Canada is concerned, the reply which the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra read into the record this morning shows that the government, feeling that there was a defence need, agreed to the cable being laid by Commercial Cable Company and to defence circuits being terminated in Canada if our existing facilities were not sufficient for defence needs.
We did say, and I shall not attempt to gloss over the matter, that if any commercial circuits were to be opened they would have to be leased to C.O.T.C. I make no apology for that, Mr. Chairman. I think that was an arrangement which accorded to the project the importance it had as a project for defence. But the truth of the matter is that the company was not satisfied to go ahead with the project unless it had these 24 circuits that would terminate in Canada. In other words, it was not sufficient for this company to have all of the business that the government of the United States was prepared to pay for, all of the United States commercial business that was there and all of the business that there was in prospect, as described in very glowing terms by Mr. Henderson, vice-president of the Commercial Cable Company, but they must also have 24 more duplex circuits terminating in Canada.
As Minister of Transport, Mr. Chairman, I have the responsibility of recommending to my colleagues in the cabinet the action that ought to be taken in that particular field of activity, and I may assure members of the

Telegraphs Act
house that I could not see my way clear to recommending the unqualified acceptance of the application of Commercial Cable to open 24 duplex circuits in Canada when the company was in receipt of a rental of $1,600,000 which represented somewhere around 65 per cent of the total operating cost, including interest. The hon. member for Oxford and others who spoke this morning suggested that there was no particular danger that might result from the fact that the Commercial Cable Company might receive $1,600,000 from the United States government. What disturbed me was that that was perhaps just the beginning of what the company might be receiving and that in the event that other circuits would be leased the amount that would be paid by the United States government would represent an unduly high proportion of the operating cost, including interest, and in effect that would mean that the facilities that the Commercial Cable Company would be providing in Canada through the 24 circuits to be terminated there would be cable service provided as a by-product of a large project financed by United States government funds.
I did not feel that I could recommend the granting of a landing permit to Commercial Cable for that particular project. As I said in the committee, I feel that we should have the opportunity to see what need there is for additional circuits when those to be opened by C.O.T.C. are made available some time in October of this year.
I should like to deal very briefly, because I do not think it is necessary to say very much about it, with the question of trying to make a monopoly of C.O.T.C. I ask hon. members to consider this simple fact. It is not necessary for the government to introduce Bill No. 212 in order to refuse applications for the landing of further cables. It is sufficient to read the express terms of section 22 of the Telegraphs Act which I should like to put on the record. Section 22 reads:
The company-
At this point I am referring to marine electric telegraph companies, the name by which these cable companies are known in the statute.
-shall not exercise any of the powers by this part conferred until
(a)	the company has submitted to the governor in council, a plan and survey of the proposed site and location of such telegraph and its approaches at the shore, and of its stations, offices and accommodations on land and of all the intended works thereto appertaining,
(b)	such plan, site and location have been approved by the governor in council, and
(c)	such conditions as he thinks fit for the public good to impose touching the said telegraph and works, have been complied with.

When we received the application of the Commercial Cable Company the deputy minister of justice was asked his opinion as to whether or not the granting of a landing permit, which is the name commonly applied to the form of permit that is given under section 22, was mandatory or not. The deputy minister replied that the question of whether the approval required by this statute is to be given by the governor in council or withheld is one to be determined by the governor in council as a matter of policy. He said that he did not find in the act any provision, express or implied, that fetters the discretion of the governor in council and that he could in his view refuse to approve the plan, site or location of the proposed cable on any ground that he considered to be in the public interest.
In other words, if, as was suggested by some of the members of the Progressive Conservative party this morning, the government desired to prevent any expansion by either Western Union or the Commercial Cable Company it would not be necessary for us to introduce Bill No. 212. All that would be necessary for us to do would be to resist, if I may use the word that the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra quoted from one of the agreements, and to refuse to grant under any conditions any applications that might be made for landing permits.

That section I think clearly implies that those are conditions that should be accomplished before the laying of the cable is completed. In other words, Mr. Chairman, they are not of the kind that I might describe as being of a continuing character, the sort of thing that happens from day to day after the cable is laid.
Let me give to the committee an example of the sort of thing I have in mind. As the situation is at present, all of the cables that have been laid-perhaps I should not say all of them but should say many of them-or many of the cables that have already been laid had a much lesser capacity for the transmission of messages than they now have. As was said by the hon. member for Wellington South, I think it was this morning, it is quite possible by the incorporation of electronic repeaters into a cable to increase materially the message carrying capacity of the cable. It could be doubled, trebled or quadrupled.
But today we do not think very much in terms of doubling the duplex circuits because the factor involved is so small. The important situation, Mr. Chairman, is this. Today we may lay a coaxial cable having a capacity, say, of 120 duplex circuits. But what is there to tell us that tomorrow or next year there may not be some developments in the equipment or in something that can be incorporated into the cable itself which will materially increase the messagecarrying capacity of that cable and create an entirely new situation, particularly in these days where governments, because of their interest in defence or world affairs, can upset the normal economics of the situation by renting-usually at fairly generous rentals-circuits.
At all events, Mr. Chairman, so far as I am concerned it seems to me that it is desirable that we should have the right, by this licensing system which is contemplated, to control the development of additional outlets. Perhaps I should not call them outlets. Perhaps I should call them additional circuits. If, for example, we start off with 24 today, as the company requested, perhaps by tomorrow that might be 120. I think that the government, speaking for the people of Canada, should have the right to decide Whether this multiplication of facilities is to take place with or without its approval.

The bill which is before the committee will enable the government to control the development of new circuits and the increase of existing circuits so that when approval is given for the laying of a cable it will be possible to prevent the capacity of the cable from being unduly increased, at least without the government being consulted.

It says that the company shall not exercise -that is the very start of operations, namely exercising their powers until the conditions have been complied with.
