subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: Did the minister not make some submission to the law officers of the crown in order to ascertain whether or not section 22, as it now exists, did not require that any conditions that are imposed should be those in the public interest or with the public interest in mind? The change that you now bring about by this amendment does away with the necessity of any regard being had for the public interest. If this bill is passed in its present form, the only regard that needs to be had is at the caprice, if you will, of the order in council, regardless of the public interest. I am asking for information.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: I will try to answer the hon. gentleman. The question that I referred to earlier was as to whether or not it was mandatory for the governor in council to grant a landing permit under section 22. The opinion, of which I read an excerpt, was from the deputy minister on that particular question as to whether or not the issue of the permit was mandatory. That is the first one. The second point is that we are not changing that situation at all. We are merely providing that there may be conditions of a continuing character as part of the condition of a licence which the company would require to have. I hope I have answered the hon. gentleman's question. I am not trying to sidestep it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: There may be conditions beyond the public interest that require you to make an order in council? Is that what the minister mean's?

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext:
No. I am not suggesting that for an instant, Mr. Chairman. I may say quite frankly that I cannot conceive of a licensing system of which the conditions were not intended to be in the public interest. I am not trying to conceal anything from the committee on that score. I think that the legislation is perfectly clear. I think we have quite wide authority to make regulations under the proposed bill in connection with a licensing system. When we get to the clause by clause study of the bill I am sure the hon. gentleman will see that. But I take it that these regulations must not, in all decency, be framed except having the public good in mind. I cannot help thinking

that, after all, the government must be responsible to parliament for the regulations that it enacts pursuant to this bill.
I should just like to say one further word, Mr. Chairman. I may not have answered all the questions that were raised. If not, I should be glad to endeavour to do so. But as I said at the second reading stage of the bill, it seems to me that it enables the government to have more flexibility in the administration of section 22 of the Telegraphs Act. As I see it now, we are faced with the necessity of choosing between a pure and simple yes or no answer to an application that may be made. I think it is very difficult for us to attach qualifications to the response that we give to an application for a landing permit. I think that the licensing system adds more flexibility and will enable the government to attach to the granting of a landing permit conditions that are of a continuing character and that extend beyond the pure operation of laying the cable and bringing it into operation.
There are just one or two things upon which I should like to touch. I think it was the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, or perhaps some other hon. member who seemed to attach great importance to the fact that, when this application was considered first of all by my department officials, Mr. Bowie, the president of C.O.T.C., and I think two or three other officials of C.O.T.C. were present at the meeting. They seemed to see something almost sinister in that. I should like to assure them there was nothing sinister about it. The rather curious point in connection with this application of Commercial Cable was that we had believed, up to that time, that the route across Newfoundland to be followed by the T.A.T. cable was known only to a very restricted group. I am not suggesting it was secret or that it had to be a secret, but we did not believe that anybody else knew about it apart from those concerned with the laying of the T.A.T. cable.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: Which cable was that, to which the minister referred?

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext:
I am talking about the transAtlantic telephone cable. When this application of Commercial Cable was received, it was a real surprise that they were proposing to follow the same route. Consequently, it was a matter of great importance to C.O.T.C. to see that the cable that was described in the application of Commercial Cable was not laid in such a way as to interfere with the T.A.T. cable. Their participation in the meeting was not only because of that fact but also because of the fact that they are

the most experienced people connected with my department in the field of cable operation.
Now, I should like to say one word about rates. No effort has been made up to the present by the government to control cable rates. As I said in the committee, the rather happy situation that exists now is because there is competition between these three companies. There has been no great difficulty about having to control rates or keeping them down. I should like to repeat, as I said in the committee, that C.O.T.C. has been a factor which has enabled us to keep the rates for cables down. There have been suggestions made at earlier dates by the two United States companies that cable rates should be increased, but C.O.T.C. has refused to accept the suggestions for increases in rates. As hon. members know, C.O.T.C. has managed, I think through the good management of Mr. Bowie and the directors and officers of the company, to operate for six consecutive years with a surplus after paying taxes and interest on the government's investment in the company. In fact, the rates which apply to cables are actually four cents per word lower on cables transmitted from Montreal than on cables transmitted from New York. I have no doubt whatever that if circumstances were such that, because of the fact that new circuits were being opened and were being, let us say, provided with ample funds by the government of the United States, they would be creating the kind of competition that would be exceedingly difficult to meet and C.O.T.C. would have a very difficult time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: Would the minister permit a question?

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. member would wait just a minute.
It has been suggested we are trying to protect C.O.T.C. If there had been another Canadian cable company, I would have been very happy about it. But if there is any protection that is being given as a result of our refusal of the Commercial Cable application or in the policies that we have discussed here I think, if anything, it has been to see that Canadian telecommunications operations are not snowed under in a field which is highly competitive and in which the competitive forces are very powerful, very large corporations with very substantial sums of capital at their disposition.
I think, Mr. Chairman, I have dealt with all the questions. There is just one it is suggested that I perhaps should touch upon and that is whether or not the issuing of licence under the bill now before the committee would be mandatory. I do not think 67509-429J
Telegraphs Act
it would be mandatory. I may say I have discussed the question with Mr. Driedger of the Department of Justice. It is naturally difficult for him to give an opinion which arises with respect to regulations which have not yet been drafted, but I have tried to assure the members of the committee that there was no intention on the part of the government to interfere with the operation of existing cable companies. I think it is very unlikely that the regulations will be drafted in such a way or that any government would administer a licensing system, so that it could arbitrarily refuse an application from any of the cable companies. I have tried to answer most of the questions, but if some of the hon. members would still like to have an answer I shall do my best to give it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: The minister has answered a number of questions that have been put to him, and I realize there were a great many. Naturally he could not answer them all at one time. There is one question.,that is still not clear to me with regard to rates. The minister has pointed out he is not very much alarmed by the $1,600,000 a year rental, which is in effect a type of subsidy, the United States government will give to Commercial Cables. But his alarm in the future might be raised-

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: I am alarmed even by the $1,600,000.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: If the minister is alarmed by that, he would be more alarmed if it were increased.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: My alarm would increase as the amount increased.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: In view of this very handsome assured income for at least 10 years, in the event that Commercial Cable Company started some kind of rate war which would involve C.O.T.C. and Western Union, what would then prevent the minister from invoking a section of the Railway Act in bringing the regulations of these telecommunication rates under the minister in the same way as railway rates are? Apparently in the past these rates have always been settled amicably by discussion, but if a rate war did start, what would then prevent that action?

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I thought that in the committee I had almost reached the point of convincing the hon. member for Oxford.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: You had for a while.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext:
I think he had slipped away from me in the committee, Mr. Chairman,

Telegraphs Act
but for a while I thought I had almost convinced the hon. member it is not just a question of the rates but that there was also the collateral question of what might be paid out to get the business, what might be paid out to advertise a particular company's advantages.
The hon. member spoke this morning about sending cables. Most of us know perfectly well that if you go to send a cable most people do not know what company it is going by. You go into the Canadian Pacific Telegraph or Canadian National Telegraph office and ask them to send your cable for you but if one of the companies receives a higher percentage of the cost of the message if they send it via Commercial or via Western Union than they do via C.O.T.C. then I think human nature being what it is the telegraph company will send it by the route which attracts the most dollars to its own treasury.
I do not think that condition existed formerly because everybody was on his own when the number of circuits in a cable was small. I think I mentioned before that the maximum was 8 simplex circuits. We are now talking about a large number of circuits of which a small proportion are going to be rented to the United States government for a rental which represents something like 65 per cent of the operating expenses of the cable.
The hon. gentleman may not be concerned by that but I think all I can say to him is that not having the responsibility for what happens to C.O.T.C. he may be indifferent as to whether it is $1-6 million or $2-6 million or $3-6 million; but having that responsibility I cannot be indifferent. As I said a moment ago my concern increases as the amount increases over $1-6 million.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I certainly appreciate, as I think all members do, the minister's high sense of responsibility and I warmly commend him for it. I am trying to establish in my own mind and for at least some hon. members of the house what the reason is.
I am now beginning to get back a little more into line with the minister's thinking again in view of his explanation in this regard but there are two things about which I am still a little unclear in relation to the subsidies. The minister said that because of this indirect form of subsidy and because of other things such as advertising and through other means business might be channelled into the Commercial Cable Corporation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: Or Western Union.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: Yes. But at the same time is it not a fact that there are only the two companies in Canada which pick up telegraphs, the Canadian National Telegraph Company and the Canadian Pacific Telegraph Company? It is my understanding, and I am open to correction on this, that Western Union carries all the messages picked up by the Canadian National Telegraphs whereas the Commercial Cable Corporation and the C.O.T.C. divide the messages that are picked up by Canadian Pacific Telegraphs.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: That is assuming there is no designation by the sender of the message.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: I think some of us are a little unclear on this matter. If you send a telegram in a Canadian National Telegraph office and specifically designate that it should go via Commercial Cable Corporation is it possible it would be sent in that way? I realize it is highly unlikely that a sender would designate.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: I not only think it is possible, I believe that is actually what is taking place.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: I see. I have one further comment. The minister is alarmed not so much by the fact of the control of rates but by what might be done through this more direct method of channelling business between the companies. I believe the point I tried to make this morning was that if this took place none of these companies, no matter how large they might be, would be foolish enough to try and engage in some kind of rate war with a crown corporation because of the loans that would be possible. I do not think any sensible private company would attempt to engage in a rate war either directly or indirectly with a crown company knowing that the resources of the Canadian government were behind the crown corporation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, dealing first with this question of rates, the impression I gained in the standing committee was that these companies including the crown company have a pretty neat little arrangement which, if it were within Canada, would probably be considered as a combine in so far as rates are concerned. I would be very much surprised if that picture does not continue into the foreseeable future. They will get together and agree upon the rates that are to be charged and then they will all charge the same rates, which is what they are doing today.
Even if the Commercial Cable company should attempt to reduce the rates, surely the Canadian businessman who uses cable services should receive the first consideration. There has not been a word said here about

the benefit to him as a result of getting a cheaper rate. The minister seems to be concerned about only one factor and that is that the crown company shall be protected.
The minister stressed that his objective was to protect this crown company and actually he is not only protecting the crown company but he is protecting its partner, the American Telephone and Telegraph Company, and its subsidiary the Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company by his actions.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: I do not think the hon. gentleman should make that suggestion because the Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company and the American Telephone and Telegraph Company are not in the cable business.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: They are not in what?

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: They are not in the cable business; they are in the telephone business. The transatlantic telephone cable is primarily a telephone operation. It is only a telegraph operation so far as half a voice circuit is concerned which I believe may be used by the United States government or others. The point I want to emphasize is that the American Telephone and Telegraph Company, and the same applies to Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company, are not in the cable business and are not competitors of any of the cable companies.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext:
The crown corporation is in partnership with the American Telephone and Telegraph Company and its subsidiary the Eastern Telephone and Telegraph Company and with the British post office. They are all in the bag together. The minister's policy obviously is to protect that group. He is stretching our credulity rather far when he asks us to believe he is only trying to protect the crown company.
The minister gave the impression today that what is proposed is a licensing system. One would think to hear him speak that it was to be an impartial licensing system under which the department would weigh the scales and see that the crown company was treated in exactly the same way as the Commercial Cable Company and Western Union and that this nice new licensing system would be just a general control system which would apply in the same way to everyone in the business; but unfortunately the facts are just the opposite.
The minister himself in his statement today has made it perfectly clear that the government plan is a plan to prevent up-to-date competition from the Commercial Cable Company and Western Union. Of course, Western Union does not enter into the picture so much because it is not trying to lay
Telegraphs Act
a coaxial cable and I believe an order has been made in the United States courts to the effect that they must divest themselves of this cable business. They are not interested in keeping up to date in the same way as is the case with the Commercial Cable Company, the other private company. What is the minister doing under this policy? Here you have his own child, the C.O.T.C., as a result of the first coaxial cable getting the equal of eleven duplex circuits. I may be wrong in those figures.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: That is what I understood the minister to say. The C.O.T.C. is to have that type of equipment in October of this year. Commercial Cable are still asking for permission to lay a cable of that type. It will take them probably several years to lay such a cable. The minister does not say, "It would be fair for C.O.T.C. to have eleven circuits and Commercial Cable to have eleven circuits," he says, "Oh, no, Commercial Cable will not have one circuit in Canada; we will not allow them to have one circuit in Canada; if they lay this coaxial cable they must continue to do business with their old cable in so far as Canada is concerned." The minister made that very clear on more than one occasion in the committee and I would refer hon. members to page 185 of the proceedings. Incidentally this is a confirmation of the stand taken by the minister in the letter which he wrote in February of 1955. I quote from page 185 of the proceedings:

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: You say that so far as the Canadian government is concerned they cannot have a coaxial cable or system, whatever it is called or described. Is that possibly the view your department is taking?

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext:
The approach which the department is taking is that the Commercial Cable Company asked for a permit to land a coaxial cable of 120 duplex circuits, and we said you may use them for defence purposes and make a connection in Canada for defence purposes, where existing facilities are not adequate, but if you open any circuits for commercial purposes you must do so by leasing them to C.O.T.C.
The minister has not varied that stand one iota; he skated all around it by talking about a licensing system but he is still standing on the policy that if these people lay a coaxial cable and place any circuits in Canada those circuits must be used for defence purposes or be leased to the C.O.T.C., which is their competitor. How that can be considered as fair is completely beyond me. One would have thought that the Department of Transport would be impartial in this matter and would have allowed each group to have an equal number of circuits, or at least to have some of the circuits. But that is not to be the case. Commercial Cable, and no doubt Western Union would be treated the same way,

Telegraphs Act
are faced with this government policy. They have been told that they cannot have any of these up-to-date circuits, that they must carry on with the old type equipment. I do not see how the minister can justify a policy of that kind. In effect it means a monopoly for the crown corporation because if these other companies cannot modernize why should they try to hang on in Canada. It certainly means that the Canadian businessman will lose the benefit of that competition.
Even if rates are the same they might be able to get better service from one company than from another. For example, I am told that in the case of a cable message from Vancouver to Japan, if it were sent by Commercial Cable it would go to Seattle and thence to Japan, whereas if it were sent by C.O.T.C. it would go across Canada to Montreal, thence to London, and thence right around the world to Japan. It takes some time longer to reach Japan going that way than it would if sent over the other system. In so far as cable service from the west coast to Australia and New Zealand is concerned, C.O.T.C. give the better service, and more credit to them for that.
Surely the businessman in Vancouver is entitled to choose the way in which his cables are to be sent. If this government policy is carried out the only service available will be by a crown company. I suggest That that is entirely unfair. Will the minister indicate who is going to be hurt by there being too many of these circuits in Canada? He seems to be greatly worried about there being more circuits than are necessary. He seems to think that somebody is going to be badly hurt if that is the case. It seems to me that the people who would not be hurt are those who send the cables. Certainly it would not do any harm to them. Just who is it that is going to be hurt if these eleven circuits belong to C.O.T.C. and 24 circuits belong to Commercial Cable or eleven circuits belong to Commercial Cable? Who is going to be hurt if there are more circuits than are required? Will it not be the companies that would suffer rather than the Canadian people? Those who are doing business would benefit.
This policy seems to be contrary to the whole trend of development in Canada. This country is opening up from coast to coast and surely the demand for this service is increasing. We were told in the committee that it was increasing very rapidly. Why should these restrictions be placed upon this development? Mr. Henderson of the Commercial Cable Company gave evidence about the business they had in prospect for the

new circuits. This will be found at page 205
of the proceedings, and I quote:
Now, with respect to Canada, we did not feel that it was necessary to make a survey here. The minister has stated that he is going to have six telegraph channels when this transatlantic cable is in operation and he has half a voice channel at his disposal. We have a demand now. in the Commercial Cable Company for five leased channels across the Atlantic, and that is even without going out trying to sell channels. We believe the people of Canada should have the opportunity to lease channels direct through to a customer in London, Paris, or wherever it may be. If you are able to dial on your telephone to London, you should be able to dial on your telegraph to London. We believe at some future time that the teleprinter will be out of date.
The minister stated that if we had made an application for a cable of two circuits, that his answer may have been different. If I had made that application I think that my board of directors would have fired me.
Will the minister please explain just who it is in Canada who is going to be hurt if there are more circuits than seem to be required at the present time?

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext:
Before the minister replies I should like to say a word. I should like to say that two months ago the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and I were on the same side in connection with a very important matter when we were trying to save Canada from the evils of turning over to powerful American-controlled corporations certain important national resources. It is somewhat embarrassing for me today to find a colleague of a few months ago on the wrong side of an important matter affecting the future of Canada.
We had a very long discussion in the committee, and there were at least three divisions. The hon. member for Hamilton West and the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, who are not here this afternoon, tested the opinion of the committee, and on the first vote there were four yeas and 19 nays, as shown on page 223 of the record. In the next vote, as shown on page 227, there were three in favour and 17 opposed. The final vote was an interesting one. The following amendment was moved:
This part does not apply in respect of a company which is already operating external submarine cables under the authority of an act of the parliament of Canada.
Had that amendment carried, it would have committed this parliament to the proposition that we are not permitted to have anything to say about the operations of Commercial Cable, as a result of certain privileges they were given 72 years ago. This motion was presented to the committee, and it is recorded:
Motion defeated. The Clerk counting.

I do not recall whether he saw any who voted for it, but there is no record as to whether or not anybody voted for this. I think that we cannot accept that proposition. The minister went over the matter very fully in the committee and again this afternoon, and I am not going to repeat it, but I think that it cannot be established that he is guilty of trying to establish a monopoly. He pointed out correctly that, because C.O.T.C. is in this field, everyone who uses cable services in Canada is able to send a cable from Canada to the United Kingdom for four cents a word less than people in New York.
The last time I was in Europe, I sent a cable home from the publicly owned post office in London and I was surprised to find that when I reached New York I had to pay more for a telegram over privately owned telegraph companies from New York to my home in Saskatchewan than I paid over the publicly owned cable and telegraph system from Canada. In other words, I spent less for that cable from London to Sturgis, Saskatchewan, than for a telegram from New York to Sturgis, Saskatchewan. So I think it cannot be argued that we have not competition in that field. We are still going to have at least Western Union, the Commercial Cable Company and C.O.T.C. I think the minister has made a convincing case that he does require the legislation that is proposed in Bill 212.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: I cannot agree with my hon. friend when he says he thinks the minister has made a convincing case. The minister always speaks with a degree of conviction and with something which appears like logic, in such a way that it does carry, not conviction but perhaps an appearance of it, to one who has not studied his statements too carefully. I must admit that I have not studied them too carefully on this occasion. I was not in the committee when the hearing was conducted on this bill, as I perhaps should have been because I was a member of the committee. However, I was not here at the time and therefore did not hear the evidence, although I have read it since. Incidentally, my hon. friend referred to the votes in the committee. I think that means very little as to the number of members that may be present, because when that committee was sitting, Mr. Chairman, as you know, there were four or five of the committees sitting at the same time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: Your party was represented.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext:
It may have been that certain people who were not present were in other committees who otherwise would have
Telegraphs Act
been there and voted for or against the amendments that were proposed. I go back again to the case the member for Vancouver-Quadra has made, which I think is a convincing case. If the minister has made one to the satisfaction of the hon. member who has just spoken, I think that the member for Vancouver-Quadra has made a more convincing one. The hon. member who preceded me has admitted that the minister made a convincing case for a monopoly. I think that was the tribute he paid to his logic, and if the minister is prepared to accept that accolade, then I shall not argue too strenuously that my hon. friend is convinced at any rate of that.
I think it is section 22 of the Telegraphs Act which at present creates powers under which the minister will have to act until this bill is passed. It refers to the public good, and any action taken under that section would have that connotation. There are no such words in the present bill, and obviously a minister can pass such regulations as are approved by his colleagues. The effect of those regulations, I think the minister will admit, would be to create a monopoly. He said a while ago, in reply to the member for Prince Albert, I think, that of course the government would be motivated by what was in the public good, but of course-

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: I think that would apply to governments of all parties, even the one my hon. friend represents.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: That goes without saying, but that would be something we have not had an opportunity to demonstrate at the moment.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: Because of the ideas you are propounding now.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext:
The expression "public good" as contained in the legislation has a specific meaning, as the minister knows, as interpreted by the courts through many years of experience. I am afraid that the expression "public good" as in the minister's mind is a much looser expression, and he qualified it afterwards by saying that he felt that his responsibility was to the C.O.T.C. Apparently his impression of public good is something which will protect the C.O.T.C., because he said that is his responsibility.
I think the member for Vancouver-Quadra emphasized another matter. I am sure the minister would not deny, although it perhaps has escaped his attention for the moment, that he also has a responsibility to the public as a whole, and what might possibly infringe upon the C.O.T.C. might conceivably be in

Telegraphs Act
the public interest. I personally cannot accept the proposition that by creating a government monopoly you are thereby promoting the public interest. After all, it was only two or three years ago that the C.P.A. made application for certain rights for carrying freight. They were denied them because apparently it was not considered in the public interest and the T.C.A. had to be protected. I am sure if that matter had been discussed years before, when T.C.A. was first incorporated or first developed and the present minister had been the minister in charge, I can see him, in a smooth, convincing manner assure one that under no circumstances was there any thought of creating a monopoly and that it would be in the public good and only in the public good.
The suggestion was made in the committee that if the regulations had to be passed the matter should be referred to the board of transport commissioners and the power vested there rather than in the minister's own department. The minister's reply to that was that he had qualified men in the department who knew of the administration of cables, that the board of transport commissioners was not qualified to handle that, and therefore it would not be in the public interest to have this matter referred to the board and dealt with by the board of transport commissioners.
If some such reservations are necessary, it is highly desirable that they be administered by an apparently independent and responsible body rather than by the minister's department itself. I think that the hon. member for Mackenzie who preceded me expressed it very succinctly when he said that the minister had made a forceful case for a monopoly. Personally I am not prepared to accept that as a desirable thing and in the public interest. There are many arguments which one could use. I could advance a local one. I noticed in the evidence that Commercial Cable suggested that if the license were granted and they laid the new cable they might operate a cable ship out of Halifax which would result in the spending of large sums of money on the east coast, up to $800,000 a year and another $250,000 a year in Newfoundland.
That is a very commendable reason and one good reason why I would be in favour of the minister reconsidering the matter and would be in favour of Commercial Cable Company being given the privileges it seeks. They are really not privileges for after all this company has been in existence since 1884. They have been carrying on since then and have given good service. They have somewhat of a vested interest in this business. Perhaps that is a disreputable term

That is the only way in which this crown company will be able to get service through the coaxial cable system. They have this agreement)with the American Telephone and Telegraph Company. So far as United States companies are concerned we are both in the same position.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: Except that we are tied in with the British government.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not expect that there would be any discussion on third reading. I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) when he says that the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hosking) is perhaps never dubious as to the policy of the present government. However, I think the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra will agree that that cannot be said about me. The thing which has surprised me about this whole matter is that apparently the Conservative party has been as gullible as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra accuses the hon. member for Wellington South of being. By that I mean to say that they seem to have swallowed holus bolus the attempt which was made by the Commercial Cable Company-I do not blame them for doing it-to use this bill as a vehicle for introducing the subject matter of a certain application they had made to the minister under the Telegraphs Act.
If there has been any debate on the merits of socialism, or public ownership versus private ownership, it has been introduced by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and his colleagues. Certainly as far as I am concerned this is not a socialist bill and certainly I am not supporting it on the ground of being a socialist.
As far as I can see, this bill is simply a licensing bill to give the government certain powers to regulate public utilities having to do with telecommunications. We do that same sort of thing in other fields and nobody has suggested that that involves socialism. I think it is confusing the issue to attempt to create the impression that the government of Canada

has suddenly swallowed holus bolus the philosophy which some of us in this corner of the house espouse simply because they have introduced this bill.
I do not think I need to say any more. I made some few remarks on second reading when the principle was under discussion and I think it was made clear at that time that we are sympathetic to the purposes of the bill. I think we have made it quite clear that as a result of the detailed and thorough discussions which took place in the committee we are now satisfied that this bill, properly administered, will be in the interests of the Canadian people.

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Marler (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING CONTROL OF SUBMARINE CABLE INSTALLATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to what has been said, particularly by members of the Progressive Conservative party. I have been interested in knowing their position and to say the least I think it has been somewhat confused and confusing. The principal ground of complaint is that because we are providing for the establishing of a licensing system for external submarine communications we are thereby attempting to turn the C.O.T.C. into a monopoly. Nothing has been said by them here today that has suggested they are in favour of a licensing system of any kind. I do not want to speak at great length, but I think the house should understand just what is the position of the Progressive Conservative party in connection with this matter.
I do not think that any member of the Progressive Conservative party, either in the standing committee or in the committee of the whole house, has failed to raise the question of the monopoly of the C.O.T.C. I want to point out briefly just what is the situation. There are 34 duplex circuits now available in trans-Atlantic cables and those 2 are operated by C.O.T.C. To speak of a monopoly when there are 2 circuits out of 34 certainly goes far beyond my understanding. What is the monopoly position of C.O.T.C. so far as Canadian business is concerned? It has 40 per cent of the business while the two United States companies have the remaining 60 per cent. Does that sound like a monopoly, when you have even less than half of the traffic? It certainly does not. My suggestion is that, whenever the name C.O.T.C. is mentioned, there is immediately from the Conservatives a response "monopoly"; but I say that the facts do not justify any such contention as that.
What have we heard today about establishing a licensing system? Nothing whatever. Yet when we were in the committee the hon. member for York West, who seemed not to be disposed to disagree with the idea of a licensing system, moved that the bill be amended and that, in place of having the
Telegraphs Act
regulations made by the governor in council, they should be made by the board of transport commissioners. So at that particular moment the Progressive Conservative party was in favour of some form of licensing, and the same clauses and conditions were set forth and the same language was used, in effect, for the amendment as will be found in subparagraphs (a) to (e) of clause 42 of the bill. At that particular moment the Progressive Conservatives were in favour of licensing. Today there has not been one word about licensing.
All that has been said has been with the object of making sure that under no circumstances whatever should anything be done that might possibly curtail the activities of Western Union and of Commercial Cable, so far as Canadian business is concerned. Nobody has suggested for a minute that the bill was to be used to interfere with Commercial Cable dealing with the business that properly belongs to it, with the United States business originating in the United States and put on the cables in New York. Nobody has ever suggested that that was going to be interfered with, but throughout the long discussion in committee what have we heard? Nothing but "For goodness' sake, do not do anything which would affect these two United States companies."
Mr. Speaker, that is not all. After having suggested a form of licensing, but under the board of transport commissioners, the Conservative party, the hon. member for York West speaking for it, then moved that a clause 3 be added to the bill. That was, of course, in the standing committee. He moved an amendment to the effect that this part of the act shall not apply in respect to a company which is already operating external submarine cables under the authority of an act of the parliament of Canada; in other words, that nothing whatever must be done to regulate the activities of the two United States companies.
I think that the great difference of opinion arising between the Progressive Conservative party and the government is that the Progressive Conservative party can think only in terms of monopoly. We have seen that there is no monopoly, and I do not think that there is any likelihood of there being one. We find that one day they are in favour of licensing; but that the next day they are not in favour of licensing. Then they conclude by saying that they do not want this to apply to the two United States companies. I leave to hon. members the task of forming their own conclusions as to the attitude of the opposition.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE BRIDGE

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Marler (Minister of Transport) moved
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE BRIDGE
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act by repealing subsection (1) of section 14A thereof as enacted at the present session of parliament and substituting the following subsection therefor:
"14A. (1) The authority may, alone or jointly or in conjunction with the St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation of the United States, construct, maintain and operate, either
(a)	a bridge over Pollys Gut in the St. Lawrence river for the passage of pedestrians, vehicles, railway trains and for other like purposes, with all necessary approaches and facilities, from Cornwall island in the county of Stormont in the province of Ontario to Massena point in the state of New York, or
(b)	a bridge over the south channel in the St. Lawrence river for the passage of pedestrians, vehicles and for other like purposes, with all necessary approaches and facilities, from Cornwall island in the county of Stormont in the province of Ontario to the United States mainland in the state of New York."
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE BRIDGE
speechtext: Will the minister be good enough to give us a statement as to the purpose of this resolution?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE BRIDGE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, hon. members of the committee will probably recall that earlier this session we adopted chapter 11 of the statutes of the present session for the purpose, among other things, of authorizing the St. Lawrence seaway authority, either alone or jointly or in conjunction with the Saint Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation of the United States, to construct, maintain and operate a bridge over Pollys Gut. Since then there have been discussions
++NAYS
Messrs:
Bell	Casselman
Blackmore	Charlton
Cardiff	Churchill


and negotiations between the Saint Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation and the New York Central Railway which have made it possible to consider what in the mind of Canadians is, I think, a much more satisfactory alternative to the bridge over Pollys Gut. I think that perhaps I might stick more closely to a memorandum I have here on the subject and perhaps, if necessary, supplement it with a few additions.
I should like to say that after considerable negotiation, and at the request of the Canadian government, the United States Saint Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation agreed to reroute the highway and New York Central Railway in the United States by means of twin bridge facilities at the Grass river lock and bridges over the Grass and Raquette rivers in order to provide uninterrupted facilities.
It was desirable to retain as short and direct a route as possible for highway traffic coming to the Cornwall area from the east by the south shore of the St. Lawrence and particularly to provide as short a route as possible for the St. Regis Indians living in a small section of Canadian territory on the south shore of the St. Lawrence that is entirely surrounded by United States territory. These Indians come to Cornwall for supplies, schools, hospitals, employment, et cetera.
During the current session, parliament passed an amendment to the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act to authorize the St. Lawrence seaway authority to join with the U.S. Saint Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation in the construction of a low level highway and railway bridge over Pollys Gut, over the western end of Cornwall island and the United States mainland.
Just at this point, Mr. Chairman, I should like to interject that it was possible to build a low level bridge over Pollys Gut because no navigation was to take place in that part of the river. Hon. members who are familiar with the geography will realize that this plays an important part in the power development but no part whatever in the development of navigation facilities.
The proposed bridge was to replace the existing span of the Roosevelt bridge over the south channel of the St. Lawrence river which has to be removed so as to allow shipping to have access to the new 27-foot Long Sault canal. At that time it was understood that the New York Central Railway would not abandon its line between Ottawa and Helena, New York. As the only possible location for a combined low level highway and railway bridge was over Pollys Gut,
31, 1956
St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act the amendment to the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act was drafted in restrictive terms accordingly.
Within the last few weeks the New York Central Railway has let it be known that a large industrial corporation is interested in acquiring as a plant site some 2,000 acres of land in the vicinity of the proposed relocated highway and rail line on the United States south shore of the St. Lawrence river to the east of the Grass river lock. The industrial corporation in question objects-and I think quite understandably-to having the railway and highway pass through the plant area. The New York Central Railway, accordingly, proposes to abandon its line between Cornwall and Helena, New York, and to service the industry by a spur line from one of its other railway lines in that area.
The U.S. Saint Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation suggested that the highway be relocated in a westerly and a southerly direction; that is to say, west of the plant area to which I have just referred. This, however, would aggravate the problem of the St. Regis Indians who would have to travel an additional six miles to Cornwall. Furthermore, it would be much more inconvenient for all traffic travelling south and east of the international boundary.
At this point, Mr. Chairman, I should like to emphasize that the proposed diversion which would have brought the highway across twin bridges at the Grass river lock on to United States territory and then crossing Pollys Gut to meet the western end of Cornwall island would have materially added to the length of the trip that Indians living in the St. Regis reservation would have to take in order to get to Cornwall, and that the proposal to which I have just referred would have added an additional six miles to a trip that was already quite long.
At this stage the St. Lawrence seaway authority, having regard to the proposals to abandon the railway line, suggested that it would be more practical and economical to build over the south channel a high level highway suspension bridge a short distance west of the site of the present bridge. This is by far the most sensible and uncomplicated approach. It is cheaper, in that the total cost to both entities would be in the neighbourhood of $8 million against more than $9 million for the original plan. It is more direct by far and generally follows the present north-south international highway route at Cornwall. It is best for the Indians and for the traffic coming to Cornwall from the east by the south shore of the St. Lawrence.
Obviously participation by the St. Lawrence seaway authority in the construction of this
6760	HOUSE OF
St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act bridge-which of course is an international bridge-would have to be authorized by parliament, and preferably at this current session, as work should be commenced during the present construction season. The proposal which is embodied in the resolution is to amend the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act to provide that the authority would share in the cost of construction and in the building of either the low level highway and railway Pollys Gut bridge, or the south channel high level highway bridge, in the event that some unforeseen development makes it necessary to return to the idea of the bridge over Pollys Gut.
Mr. Chairman, I do not think that anybody who is familiar with the geography of this particular part of the river and the surrounding country would have any doubt whatever that the high level bridge for highway traffic over the south channel south of Cornwall island has many obvious advantages, apart from the fact that it means a lesser cost to provide these facilities than that of those which were contemplated at Pollys Gut. I have no hesitation in urging the committee to adopt the resolution to the end that, as soon as possible, we can introduce the requisite legislation based on the resolution. In that connection I should like to tell hon. members that the bill itself will contain nothing more than the strict terms of the resolution which is now before the committee.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE BRIDGE
speechtext: In view of the minister's statement, Mr. Chairman, there are just a few brief questions 1 should like to ask him. The first one is this. It is indicated in the memorandum to which the minister was referring a few minutes ago that in future there will be a high level bridge-I presume it will be a highway bridge only-over the north channel. Is that contemplated in this resolution?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE BRIDGE
speechtext: I do not think I mentioned that, Mr. Chairman. I notice that the newspapers have mentioned the possibility of a bridge over the north channel. I did not remember that I had mentioned it. I will say this, however. I think it is a perfectly logical development, although when it will be undertaken is an entirely different matter. I think it is a logical development for one to expect to take place in due time.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE BRIDGE
speechtext: The only reason I asked the question is this. It is my understanding that in the north channel there is not likely to be any shipping of any kind. I was wondering just what was the purpose of building a high level bridge over there.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE BRIDGE
speechtext:
I should not like to dismiss, quite as simply as that, the possibility that there would be no navigation in the north


channel. If my hon. friend will look at the plan of the seaway he will see that the channel for navigation is to be dredged in the south channel, that is in the waters to the south of Cornwall island, and will lead directly to the Grass river lock which is being built by the United States seaway corporation. It may well happen at some later date that Canada will decide to construct locks on its own side of the international boundary line and in that event the channel to the north of Cornwall island, the so-called north channel, would have to be used in order to provide access to the lock which I think would be located just about-I do not know if my hon. friend is familiar with the work, but at the point where there is to be what is called a structure in the dam. So ultimately if there were duplicate facilities provided for shipping it would necessitate a high level bridge over the north channel, if one is to be built.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE BRIDGE
speechtext: I take it from the minister's comments that there is no additional high level bridge contemplated over the north channel in the immediate future. I believe the present bridge, which is called the Roosevelt bridge, over the north channel will be used in the meanwhile.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE BRIDGE
speechtext: Yes, that is correct.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE BRIDGE
speechtext: There are only one or two other questions I should like to ask. In the last few days there has been considerable criticism in the press from Mr. Robert Moses, chairman of the New York power authority, claiming that if this bridge is constructed it will result in a delay of one year in the construction of the seaway. I have a number of press clippings in front of me to that effect, but I have not been able to find in any of them any reasons given by Mr. Moses for this suggested delay of a year. Nevertheless, I ask the question because a person with Mr. Moses' knowledge of the subject must know what he is talking about, and he is chairman of an important New York state authority. I was wondering if the minister would care to comment on that?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE BRIDGE
speechtext:
I should like to dispose of two points. With regard to the north channel bridge, I think the hon. gentleman will find, if he rereads the amendments which were adopted earlier this year, that they contain the necessary authority for the St. Lawrence seaway authority to build the north channel bridge if it were considered desirable that it should do so.
The second point is that I know Mr. Moses has said the building of the bridge in this new location, that is over the south channel as opposed to Pollys Gut, would have the

effect of delaying the opening of the seaway. All I can tell the committee is that the Hon. Lionel Chevrier, who is president of the St. Lawrence authority, has assured me that the question has been given most careful consideration by their technical advisers and they do not subscribe to the view which Mr. Moses has expressed that a high level highway bridge over the south channel will delay the opening of the seaway. I believe that opinion is likewise shared by the officials of the United States Saint Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE BRIDGE
speechtext: Apparently the officials of Ontario hydro have not expressed views similar to those of Mr. Moses, nor have the other two authorities concerned with the building of the seaway, but in view of the fact Mr. Moses holds a very important position can the minister give us any idea as to the type of objection Mr. Moses made and why this delay would occur? Were any suggestions ever forwarded to Mr. Chevrier?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE BRIDGE
speechtext: I do not believe Mr. Chevrier has received any communications from Mr. Moses. I would merely suggest to the hon. member for Oxford that if he were interested in the development of the park and parkways in the state of New York, he would be delighted if this bridge were going to be built over Pollys Gut thereby bringing into the United States parkways system, and to the development that will probably take place in and around the United States portion of the seaway, all of the traffic that would be crossing from Cornwall. I think if I were in the position of Mr. Moses I would probably be most anxious to have the bridge built over Pollys Gut. But as I have no responsibility for parks or parkways in New York, I should like to see it where it would do the most good for the Indians on the St. Regis reserve.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE BRIDGE
speechtext:
After having heard the comments of the minister and having taken a good look at a map of the area, I think I see what he means.
There is one other question I should like to ask. In the memorandum to which the minister referred, it was stated that this proposed new high level bridge over the south channel would cost $8 million whereas the other one over Pollys Gut would cost $9 million. In other words, the second one would cost about a million dollars less even though one would normally think a high level bridge would cost more. However, this proposed high level bridge only involves highway traffic, whereas the first bridge involves railway traffic as well as highway traffic.

St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE BRIDGE
speechtext: Yes, that is quite right.

Are there any additional
amounts for which the authority would be responsible besides the $8 million to be expended on the bridge?

There are greater savings, however, than the $8 million or $9 million figures would seem to indicate. If the hon. gentleman is speaking particularly about the original plan, I think the amount of highway relocation that is involved in bringing the traffic from the bridge over the north channel to the new bridge over the south channel is less and, inasmuch as there is no railway relocation, there are some substantial advantages.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE BRIDGE

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE BRIDGE

The costs are to be divided between the two authorities. I know of no other costs in connection with this particular aspect of the seaway construction program than are covered by the $8 million.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE BRIDGE
speechtext: I have one more question. Since the New York Central railway line between Ottawa and Cornwall is apparently to be abandoned-I understand this railway in the past has normally carried wood products from Ottawa and coal-what will the effect be on the upper end of the Ottawa valley of an arrangement of this sort?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE BRIDGE
speechtext: The first point I should like to emphasize is that the abandonment of that section of line can only be undertaken after an application has been made to the board of transport commissioners and approved by the board. The second point I should like to make is that there has been no passenger service provided over that portion of the line for a very long time. There is, I understand, a very small volume of freight carried over it. My understanding of the matter is that it has been an uneconomic line so far as the New York Central is concerned.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE BRIDGE
speechtext:
In other words, there will be a substitute service.
